Description:
Octagonal Ch'ing-pai vessel with small curved handle and short spout. It has a short neck and flat unglazed base. The lid is missing. The vessel is decorated in relief with a floral spray on each side above a border of foliate petal panles, centred by three beads set in a triangle. The porcelain body is covered by a transparent pale blue glaze, with the exposed paste of its flat base having a rusty hue due to firing. 
Glaze is closer to Shu-fu than the typical Ch'ing-pai which is clear, transparent, pale blue and thin.
Curatorial Notes: Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu (The Williams Collection of Far Eastern Ceramics, Ann Arbor, 1972). Uthara. 2/7/05.

Description: Small blue-and-white balingbing-shaped/ octagonal jar decorated with grayish-blue stylized floral sprays, related in style to the decoration on the jar with UMMA Catalogue no. 48098. The jar has a porcelain body and a transparent pale blue glaze. The flat, unglazed base has a rusty tinge. There are two small loops near the neck of the jar. 14th century.
Curatorial Notes: Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu. {Kamer Aga-Oglu, 'The Williams Collection of Far Eastern Ceramics', Ann Arbor, 1972}. Uthara. 02/11/05.

Description:
This small bowl of Shu-fu ware has a white compact porcelain body, a flaring rim, a low sturdy foot and a slightly convex base culminating in a small knob. It is covered with an opaque pale blue glaze, except for the base and foot-rim which show a grayish-white paste. 
 
The glossy grayish-blue glaze is closer to Ch'ing-pai, but its shape and especially the foot rim and knob of clay in the center of the base is Shu-fu. This piece proves once again the close relationship that exists between the Ch'ing-pai, Shu-fu and early Black and White of the Yuan period.
Curatorial Notes:
Four almost identical Shu-fu cups, twp plain and two with cobalt blue decoration, are in the Philippine Collection of the Museum of Anthropology {Kamer Aga-Oglu, "The Realtionship Between the Ying-Ch'ing, Shu-Fu and Early Blue and White", 'Far Eastern Ceramic Bulletin', No. 8 (December, 1949), pp. 27-33, pl. V, figs. 2-4}.
Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu (The Williams Collection of Far Eastern Ceramics, Ann Arbor, 1972). Uthara. 2/8/05.

Curatorial Notes: Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu.

Description:
This Sawankhalok jar of rounded shape and low foot has a gray body and a dark brown glaze. 
This type of Siamese pottery was evidently influenced by the brown-glazed ware of the Khmer potters of neighbouring Cambodia. The brown glazed ware of Sawankhalok has been called Chaliang or Chalian ware, after the early Thai name of the district of Sawankhalok.
Curatorial Notes:
Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu ('The Williams Collection of Far Eastern Ceramics', Ann Arbor, 1972}. Uthara. 04/07/05.
The names of the two major pottery centers of Siam (Thailand), Sawankhalok and Sukhothai, are transliterated by Spinks as Svargaloka and Sukhodaya according to their graphic spelling {C. N. Spinks, 'The Ceramic Wares of Siam', Bangkok, 1965, pp. VI, 112, 119, passim.}.

The decoration is on the inside only, showing a fish in relief biscuit, surrounded by sketchy water plants painted in a soft grayish-blue. See also UMMA Catalogue No. 48124. 
15th century Ming.  
Found in Morong.

Description: Blue-and-white small cup decorated on the outside with sketchy foliage.  Late Ming.

Curatorial Notes: Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu.

Description:
Blue-and-white hollow based saucer, i.e. the base is hollow and there is no foot rim (See also UMMA Catalogue Nos. 48124, 48058, 48120, 48107). The porcelain body is covered with a bluish-white translucent glaze, except for a band around the edge of the hollowed base, where the paste has turned orange at the junction of body and glaze. 
The decoration on the exterior consists of a band of pointed petals and a border of dotted line. The inside of the dish has on the bottom a wheel shaped rosette and a band of sketchy floral motifs on the cavetto. 
First half of the 15th century.
Curatorial Notes:
Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu ('The Williams Collection of Far Eastern Ceramics', Ann Arbor, 1972}. Uthara. 03/18/05.
Dishes of the type seen in UMMA Catalogue Nos. 48124, 48058, 48120, 48107, 48130, 48070, 48134, which we have defined as 'hollow-based', were termed 'hole-bottom' by Dr. H. Otley Beyer (Walter Robb, "New Data on Chinese and Siamese Ceramic Wares of the 14th and 15th Centuries", 'Philippine Magazine', XXVII, 1930, Fig. 10). Description:
This porcelain bowl of 'Lien-tzŭ' shape has slightly curved sides, straight rim and low foot. The decoration painted in grayish-blue shows on the exterior a band of petals near the foot and a border of waves at the rim. On the inside there is at the bottom a conch shell reserved in white on a ground of blue wave design, with a single ring band circling the rim. A slightly bluish white transparent glaze covers the bowl, except the tip of its foot-rim. The mouth rim and edge of the foot-rim are slightly chipped. 
Early 15th century. 
 
Bought from Castro.  Found in Palawan.
Curatorial Notes:
This porcelain bowl, although of a simpler variety, represents a distinct type of blue and white bowls which are called 'Lien-tzŭ' (lotus pod) because they resemble it in shape. All of these bowls, regardless of the variation in their decoration, have on the outside the familiar band of petals, with most of them showing a wave border around the outer or inner side of the rim. Some of these bowls have the Hsüan Tê mark (1426-1435).
See Garner, 'Oriental Blue and White' (London, 1954), p. 23, pl. 30c, Lien-tzu bowl with Hsuan Te mark; Pope, 'Chinese Porcelains from the Ardebil Shrine' (Washington, 1956), p. 86, pls. 46,47; idem, 'Ming Porcelains in the Freer Gallery of Art' (Washington, 1953), fig. 3; Valenstein, "Ming Porcelains: A Retrospective", 'Catalogue of a Loan Exhibition, China Institute in America', pl. 5, p. 33.

Description:
This Sawankhalok celadon dish has a flattened rim with raised edge and low foot. It has an incised decoration on the inside, consisting of a wave-band below the rim and two concentric rings on the bottom. The exterior is fluted and the glaze which covers it down to the foot is of an olive green. The exposed paste of the foot and base has turned a reddish-pink. 
Purchased from Peng Seng.
Curatorial Notes:

The names of the two major pottery centers of Siam (Thailand), Sawankhalok and Sukhothai, are transliterated by Spinks as Svargaloka and Sukhodaya according to their graphic spelling {C. N. Spinks, 'The Ceramic Wares of Siam', Bangkok, 1965, pp. VI, 112, 119, passim.}.

Description:
Sawankhalok (Sisatchanalai) celadon glazed stoneware bowl with a flaring rim and fluted side. It has an incised decoration on the inside, showing a band of waves at the rim and a stiff rosette in the center of the bottom. Its grayish-green glaze stops above the foot, with the unprotected paste being nurnt brick red. On the base is the circular mark of the kiln support. 
 
Purchased from Peng Seng. 
 
This vase and the other vessels in this group (UMMA Catalogue Nos. 48174, 48165, 48151, 48166, 48149, 48053, 48095, 47963, 47962, 47968) are similar in body and glaze, style of decoration and technique of potting and firing. A characteristic feature of the ware is a dark circular mark, seen on the bases of most of the vessels, that was left by a tubular kiln support on which they rested during firing. This group of vessels represents a large family of the celadon ware of Thailand that was influenced by the famous celadon of China. The ware was made in the kiln center of Sawankhalok (Sisatchanalai) during the height of its production which, according to Spinks, extended from the early 14th to the mid 15th century.
Curatorial Notes:
Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu ('The Williams Collection of Far Eastern Ceramics', Ann Arbor, 1972}. Uthara. 03/30/05.
The names of the two major pottery centers of Siam (Thailand), Sawankhalok and Sukhothai, are transliterated by Spinks as Svargaloka and Sukhodaya according to their graphic spelling {C. N. Spinks, 'The Ceramic Wares of Siam', Bangkok, 1965, pp. VI, 112, 119, passim.}.

Si Satchanalai is now used to reference the larger production area for Sawankhalok wares, in reference to the ancient town near which the kilns were located; cms 3/15; see also https://seasianceramics.asia.si.edu

Description:
This Sukhothai bowl with flaring rim and low foot has a very coarse, gritty dark grey stoneware body which is typical of Sukhothai wares. The dark body is coated with a grayish-white slip over which there is a decoration in brown, showing sketchy grass motifs on the outside and a wheel shaped rosette in the center of the bottom, bordered by a row of uneven bars. 
 
Purchased from Peng Seng. 
 
The brown painted stoneware like this specimen differs greatly from that of Sawankhalok (See UMMA Catalogue No. 48155) in having a much coarser, gritty body which is also darker in colour. This is proved by the sherds collected from the sites of these kiln centers by Dr. John A. Pope and presented to the Museum of Anthropology for study.

Description:

Description:
This Blue and White drinking vessel of 'kendi' shape has a bulging body, short neck with protruding collar, and a bulbous spout. Stiff leaves decorate the neck, while the spout is covered with lotus scrolls. The unglazed paste of the base and foot-rim is burnt orange. The decoration of this vessel is painted skillfully in a warm purplish blue. 
Lot purchase from Indonesia.   
First half of the 15th century.

Description:
Covered blue-and-white ware box with low foot rim. It is glazed on both sides, except for the base and the rim where the cover rests. Only the cover is decorated showing four units of sketchy plant motifs. The decoration is skillfully rendered with delicate brush strokes in a pale blue. 
15th century 
Lot purchase from Indonesia. 
This bowl and the other pieces in this group (See UMMA Catalogue Nos. 48192, 48201, 48178, 48193) are similar in body and glaze, technique of potting and firing. Some of the pieces show a wash of brown slip on their bases which is a characteristic feature of the wares of Annam. These vessels are typical examples of the Annamese blue-and-white porcelain which was influenced by the early Ming blue-and-white ware of the fifteenth century because of their affinity to the well known Annamese bottle of the Topkapi Sarayi Müzesi in Istanbul which bears a date corresponding to 1450.

Description:
Small Blue and White ware jar with rounded sides, short neck and foot.  Decorated with two peach sprays on the shoulder, below which is a wide band of scrolling vine. Description:
Small Blue and White porcelain "box" with cover (2 pieces) has a low foot rim and is glazed entirely, except the edge of the foot and the interior rims of the cover and base. 
 
 The decoration rendered in pale, purplish-blue under a clear glaze, shows on the cover a cormorant, swimming among lotus flowers. The side of the box has two clusters of blade like water plants. 
16th century (Chia Ching). 
Lot purchase from Indonesia.

Description:

Description:
This porcelain ewer has a pear shaped body flattened on each side, a flaring cup-shaped mouth and low foot. A dark blue glaze covers the exterior, while the inside of the mouth and the base have a grayish-white glaze. Its spout and handle have been repaired and are a slightly lighter shade of blue glaze. 
16th century. 
Lot shipment from Indonesia.
Curatorial Notes: Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu ('The Williams Collection of Far Eastern Ceramics', Ann Arbor, 1972}. Uthara. 03/22/05.

Description:
The bowl has a flaring rim and a high slender foot. 
 
On the exterior is a depiction of a garden scene with children at play. On the bottom inside is the figure of a child. The decoration is rendered in a grayish-blue under a transparent glaze. 
 
The subject of children playing in a garden was popular in the decoration of both the marked Imperial and the ordinary Blue and White of the 15th and 16th centuries. 
 
Lot shipment from Indonesia.
Curatorial Notes:
Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu ('The Williams Collection of Far Eastern Ceramics', Ann Arbor, 1972}. Uthara. 03/18/05.

Curatorial Notes: Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu.

Description:
This blue-and-white ware jar of squat form with short neck and low foot is glazed entirely except the base. The decoration, rendered in dark and light blue, shows overlapping petals on the neck, below which is a band of lotus flowers and foliage, bordered by sketchy scrolls near the foot. 
15th century. 
 
Lot purchase from Indonesia. 
 
This bowl and the other pieces in this group (See UMMA Catalogue Nos. 48193, 48201, 48178, 48175) are similar in body and glaze, technique of potting and firing. Some of the pieces show a wash of brown slip on their bases which is a characteristic feature of the wares of Vietnam. These vessels are typical examples of the Annamese blue-and-white porcelain which was influenced by the early Ming blue-and-white ware of the fifteenth century because of their affinity to the well known Annamese bottle of the Topkapi Sarayi Müzesi in Istanbul which bears a date corresponding to 1450.
Curatorial Notes:
Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu ('The Williams Collection of Far Eastern Ceramics', Ann Arbor, 1972}. Uthara. 03/30/05.

Description:
This spherical Blue and White ware inturning globular lidded bowl with a wide mouth and flat base has a fine-grained creamy-white porcelain body, covered with a transparent glaze except the base which shows a smooth cream coloured paste. The decoration, painted in a soft grayish-blue, shows below the mouth rim a border of scrolls which is remniscent of that seen in the Chinese blue-and-white porcelain of the early Ming period. The main body is decorated with sketchy flowers and foliage, bordered by a band of scrolls near the base. 
 
The foliage decorated lid has a knob handle with brown slip visible on the lid interior 
 
15th century. 
Lot shipment from Indonesia. 
 
This bowl and the other pieces in this group (See UMMA Catalogue Nos. 48192, 48201, 48178, 48175) are similar in body and glaze, technique of potting and firing. Some of the pieces show a wash of brown slip on their bases which is a characteristic feature of the wares of Annam. These vessels are typical examples of the Vietnamese blue-and-white porcelain which was influenced by the early Ming blue-and-white ware of the fifteenth century because of their affinity to the well known  bottle of the Topkapi Sarayi Müzesi in Istanbul which bears a date corresponding to 1450.
Curatorial Notes:

Description:
Square Ch'ing pai colored saucer with a fine porcelain body and transparent glaze. It is decorated with the figures of two fishermen, one in a boat and the other reclining on the shore under a willow tree. The designs are rendered in red, green, yellow and lavender enamels, with some of the details traced in fine black lines. 
Late 16th, early 17th centuries. 
Purchased from Marchant.
Curatorial Notes: Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu ('The Williams Collection of Far Eastern Ceramics', Ann Arbor, 1972}. Uthara. 03/22/05.

Description:

On the exterior are five knobs near the rim and on the unglazed center of the bottom is a floral spray in relief which is burned red.    
Purchased from Marchant.
Curatorial Notes: Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu ('The Williams Collection of Far Eastern Ceramics', Ann Arbor, 1972}. Uthara. 03/29/05.

Description: Shallow, white porcelain bowl on a foot ring with painted polychrome decorations in green, red and yellow- four alternating flower and geometric designs in band near rim and single flower with plant in center. Small chip on rim.

Description:
Shallow blue and white bowl with stencil design inside (of stylized Arabic script) and unglazed ring around center.  Low ring base with unglazed base interior and scraping marks clearly visible.

Late Ming Dynasty, 17th century.
Curatorial Notes: Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu.

Description:
White glazed dish with unglazed ring around center and overglaze red designs- four alternating hatched and stylized designs on sides inside and single stylized design in center.  
Late Ming,17th century.
Curatorial Notes: Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu.

Description:
Blue and white dish with unglazed ring around center and four stencilled designs near rim inside and single one off-center on bottom.   There are two smaller stencilled elements and traces of a third  on the vessel exterior near rim.  Traces of coarse sand adhere to the base exterior. 
 
Late Ming, 17th century.
Curatorial Notes: Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu.

Description:
Blue and white chilin dish with foliated rim.  Botanical motif on interior base, and decorative band around rim interior. 
 
The white glaze is greenish and the blue faded. Glaze damaged due to sea water. 
 
Purchased from Max Umpar.
Curatorial Notes: Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu.

Description:
Small undecorated Ch'ing-pai dish with straight unglazed rim. It has a very low rounded foot-rim and is covered with a bluish-white glaze which stops at an uneven line above the base. The exposed rim, lower portion of the sides, and the base show a white paste. 
Purchased from Estrada. 
See also UMMA Catalogue no. 48016.
Curatorial Notes:
The Sung Ch'ing-pai, the forerunner of the Yuan Shu-fu, was evidently made during both periods in numerous kiln centers of southern China, particularly in the provinces of Kiangsi, Fukien, Chekiang and Kuangtung. (Feng Hsien-ming, "Important Finds of Ancient Chinese Ceramics Since 11949", 'Wen Wu', 1965, No. 9}

Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu ('The Williams Collection of Far Eastern Ceramics', Ann Arbor, 1972}. Uthara. 02/11/05.

Description:
Northern celadon two eared jarlet with underglaze raised white floral design around shoulder and stylized design around the bottom. 
Purchased from Angle Ednaco.
Curatorial Notes: Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu.

Description:
Large shallow porcelain dish with white slip decoration on blue ground. It has a low foot and an unglazed base burnt red. Around the inner side of the foot rim are heavy accretions of kiln sand. The dish has a rather coarse white porcelain body, a blue glaze and is decorated on the inside with delicate flowers in white slip which are rendered in dots, drops and fine lines. 
 
Second half of the 16th century.   
 
Purchased from Ongpin.
Curatorial Notes:
Description derived from the research of Kamer Aga-Oglu ('The Williams Collection of Far Eastern Ceramics', Ann Arbor, 1972}. Uthara. 03/21/05.
A similar dish is found in the Philippine Collection of the Museum of Anthropology {Kamer Aga-Oglu, "The So-Called 'Swatow' Wares: Types and Problems of Provenance", 'Far Eastern Ceramic Bulletin', VII, No. 2, 1955, fig. 34}.

Spear with long wooden shaft.  At the bottom, the shaft is carved down a little, allowing a metal cap to fit over it.  The cap is a metal cone with the open end fitting over the shaft and the other end tapering down.  At the other end, the shaft is wrapped in alternating sections of rattan, with two small and one large section made of thin woven rattan in a natural color, and with two sections made of thick strips or red colored rattan, wound around.  Above that is a metal ferrule that secures the haft point of the blade to the shaft.  The blade has two barbs that angle out and down from the base, which is narrow, and then widens out to an elongated, triangular shaped blade that tapers to a point.  The blade is coated with a glossy, yellow substance.

Spear with long wooden shaft that tapers toward the bottom end.  That end is capped with a small metal tip that tapers to a point. A metal ferrule secures the point where the blade attaches to the shaft. one war spear with bilaterally recurved barbs.  Shaft wrapped in braided rattan. 


Spear with long wooden shaft.  At the proximal end the shaft is carved down, tapering to a point.  It probably once had a metal cap piece inserted over it, as seen on some of our other Philippine spears.  At the distal end, the shaft is partially carved down and sections of rattan wrap around these depressed areas.  There are three sections  of natural colored, thin, woven rattan, and one section of thicker red rattan simply wrapped around the shaft.  Past this is a metal ferrule fitted over the shaft into which the tan of the point/blade is inserted.  The blade has two barbs that extend down and out from the base.  The blade is large, tapering to a point, with both edges sharp.

The point is made of iron and is triangular in shape, with two sets of two barbs extending down and out.

Long wooden shaft narrowing to a point. A metal cone caps the end.

One spear.  Wooden shaft has a spiraling pattern of metal inlay, consisting of many small lines of metal, which covers about 2/3 of the shaft.  At the proximal end a pointed metal cap is fitted over the wood.  At the proximal end the wood widens out and is then carved down where the tang of the point inserts.  This section is secured with a metal ferrule.  A nail also goes through the wood shaft before the ferrule, probably also to secure the tang.  The point has a very long tang/shaft that extends into a wide, triangular point with two sharp barbs extending down and slightly out from its base.

Description:
This is a loose collection of miscellaneous items, assorted beads.  Most of the beads are strung on one of five short segments of blue cord.  These beads are all seeds, mostly brown but some gray.  The brown seeds are bulbous at one end and taper down to a blunt tip at the other. 

There is also a section of bamboo with fiber wrapped around it; also some wood.  The blue cord is cotton string. All stored in an envelope.
A pair of antlers which are still attached to part of the skull.

This is a cone-shaped basket made of woven rattan.  The large, round end is open so that things could be put in it.  Three dark brown bands of three rows each of rattan have been woven around the basket at irregular intervals to provide decoration.

The rattan stick is shod with an iron tip.  The shaft is decorated with 5 small  rattan rings arranged in cross (x) pattern.  The rattan skin of the upper end is removed to make a rough surface for easy grasping.

Small wood tripod object, Upon a base of two small square pieces of wood, one stacked upon the other, three thin dowels have been glued in a triangular pattern on one side while a spire has been fitted into the other.  The spire consist of a long pointed end, set and glued into a wider ribbed dowel.
The stick is made of hard wood and is sharpened at the lower end, tapered to a point.  There are 12  rings of rattan arranged in cross pattern to strengthen the stick.

Very long, thin textile of hand-woven white linen.  It is probably a table runner.  There are tassels at both ends as well as three stripes of red, green, and yellow at each end.  The cloth is quite thin and delicate.

Rectangular piece of cloth of heavy navy and white-striped pattern sewn together from three pieces.  Stripes are sewn together with pattern of alternating faded navy and red zigzag thread which is also stitched over the two short ends.  Each navy stripe has a thin red line in the center.

Small shirt made from beige/natural cotton.  There are 2 strips of cloth, each edged in dark blue, stitched together and folded over to create front and back of shirt.  Stitching is in red and blue thread with a zigzag design.

Large rectangular faded black textile with alternating 2 white and 2 red tassels on both ends.  A series of lengthwise white and red pinstripes (for the most part each stripe is a combination of a red and white stripe placed next to each other.)  There are 2 white pinstripes without red but with a series of square 1cm dots lining either side of them.  Also there are 2 red stripes with white dots lining them along with 2 wider (2cm) red stripes.  The spacing between stripes varies from 4 to 12 cm.  The larger spaces contain a design/pattern consisting of white figures and square 1 cm white dots which combine to form triangular shapes.

Long rectangular textile--hand woven, but machine sewed at ends.  Sift thread.  Multicolored striped patterning.  Colors are navy, fusia, yellow, green, slate blue, brown, and white.  A wide fusia stripe down the center has a striped line of yellow brown and beige.  On either side of fusia band are identical stripes containing smaller irregular stripes of all colors mentioned above.  On either side of center stripes are three navy stripes interspersed with multicolored stripes.

Long strip of fabric with tassels and a border at each end.  Main segment is dark blue, while borders are red, yellow, and blue.  Tassels are red and yellow thread on the ends of blue knotted and twisted thread.

Long strip of fabric with borders and tassels at each end.  Red background with 4 pairs of yellow lines.  Just before border on each end is a white and yellow zigzag pattern.  Border is a plaid pattern of yellow and blue.  Tassels are loose red and yellow threads.

Large rectangular textile--maybe hand woven.  Thread is stiff and of the following colors: fusia, navy, yellow, mint green, light blue, and white.  Mid section has a large band of fusia with a multi-color banded striped down the center and on either side.  The center band is flanked on either side by 3 solid navy stripes, alternating with 3 multi-colored bands of stripes.  The long sides are edged with wide bands of fusia.  One corner is folded and stitched.

Long rectangular cloth of six strips of blue and red-pink fabric.  The body is predominantly blue stripes (4 strips of fabric) and the ends are horizontal stripes of red-pink, blue, and white, that are slightly too long for the body.  The strips are sewn together with yellow and pink-red thread, which also comprises the tassels.  The tassels are sewn facing inward in one direction and outward in the other.  The end is stitched together on the side where the tassels face inward.  Signs of foreign deposits and insect damage.

Quiver made of multiple connected parts.  One end is a long, hollow tube, made of 1 piece of leather sewed together with fiber.  The other end is a rectangular pouch with one end left open and slightly rounded.  Arrow shafts insert into the tube end and points into the pouch end.  It is set up so that the shaft has to go in first, and only then can the point be pushed into the pouch.  This method keeps the arrows in the quiver.  A leather strap is attached to each part, and they are stitched together with cotton string.  The straps are attached to the tube and pouch with fiber cord.  Fiber string is also used to sew up the sides of the pouch.  The leather strap also has a tangled length of tan colored suede type leather wrapped around it.  The rest of the item is dark brown.

Curatorial Notes: 3/2008 - An excellent specimen of bronze cannon or swivel gun used by the Moros on their war vintas (boats), in their cotta (fortified points) and in open fighting. Obtained from Datu Sali - a local chief at lake Lanao, Mindinao, in 1938, who stated that he had obtained it in Calarian, a barrio some eight kilometers north of Zamboango, "about twenty-five years ago", with the story that it had been used in the days of piracy and fighting between the Moros and Spanish in Mindinao, the Strights of Basilian and the Sulu Islands.

Curatorial Notes: This bowl is said to be made from "nansisu" - a tree not yet identified. The bowl is ancient. They say is dates back to "The Four Lodges." The time of "The Four Lodges", i.e. four ceremonial lodges, is a time often referred to by Arikaras as a time of power and prosperity of their nation, on the Grand River or even lower down the course of their nortward migration. This bowl was purchased by Melvin R. Gilmore from Bearsbelly at Armstrong on the Ft. Berthold Reservation, August 18, 1921. It belonged to the mother-in-law of Bearsbelly, who died in 1905.

Curatorial Notes: The Cebu, Philippines Collection was collected by Domingo A. Madulid (curator of the Botanical Division of the National Museum of the Philippines), Lolita Bulalacao, and Masao Nishimura in October and Novermber 1986 on the island of Cebu in the Philippines. Specimens were collected as a collaborative effort in an attempt to correlate pollen from core samples with current vegetation to reconstruct Cebu's environment in prehistoric eras. Pressed specimens were collected from estuaries throughout Cebu, and were referenced in Masao Nishimura's University of Michigan PhD thesis, "Long Distance Trade and the Development of Complex Societies in the Central Philippines: The Cebu Central Settlement Case" submitted in 1992. Nishimura outlines a biased sampling method, with plants collected from inland, costal, swamp, and delta-inlet micro-environments (Nishimura: 1992, pgs. 164-166).. Several specimens are directly referenced in Table 3.2a-b in Nishimura's thesis (pgs. 167-168). Specimens are not mounted to herbarium sheets (A.S.1/24/2011).

One fighting spear and scabbard.  Captured in Taraca District, used in fighting Americans. 


Spear made with long bamboo (or other segmented wood) shaft.  The upper section of the shaft is enclosed by a metal tube with three raised sections of decorative bands.  This probably serves as a ferrule.  A few other sections of the shaft near this end are wrapped with rattan bands and with fiber cord.  A metal wire wraps around the shaft in a few places and runs the length of the shaft near the top, winding around itself in  sections.  Attached to that end of the shaft is a metal head with a thicker base and a generally elongated triangular shaped blade that tapers to a point.  The metal head has been coated with something that makes it glossy.

Part of a set of bow, quiver, and arrows. 


Quiver.  Made of one natural segment of bamboo so that the closed, natural growth ring node forms the base of the quiver.  The mouth is open.  From the base, a long sliver of the adjacent segment is left attached, tapers toward the end.  A curved wooden handle is attached to the middle of the quiver.  Ends of the handle tied in place by woven rattan (or possibly fiber) cord.  Their lashing is covered with an unknown black substance.
Curatorial Notes: Only quiver and bow found thus far.  2/2008.

Materials: Wood; Rattan; Bamboo; Cotton; Unknown; Fiber
Description:
Part of a set of bow, quiver, and arrows. 


One bow made of wood, three sections of which (center and midpoints between the center and the ends)  are wrapped with rattan.  The center and one of the other sections are covered over with an unknown material (possibly an animal skin?).  The center has a raised spot, probably to serve as a grip.  The bow is slightly curved and tapers toward the ends.  One end has a single carved groove; the other has several.  At the end with several, there is a loop made of fiber and purple cotton cord that connects a bamboo bowstring to the bow.  At the other end, the bowstring has broken and is no longer attached, though the fiber and cotton loop is still attached to the bow.
Curatorial Notes: Only quiver and bow found thus far.  2/2008.

1 bow, quiver, and arrows.  Bow and quiver used by mountain tribes and captured from them, Dec 20, 1904 near Perud Cata.  The heads of the arrows are poisoned. 


Long quiver made of a segment of bamboo such that the natural node growth ring forms the closed base of the quiver container.  From the base, the adjoining segment of bamboo has been shaped such that a long, slightly curved blade-like portion extends downwards, tapering to a point -- ie most of the segment has been cut away, leaving a sliver. 


Incised designs in a band on exterior of the base.  Metal handle tied in place by lengths of rattan and woven rattan bands.  The rattan is covered in clear pigment/substance almost like lacquer.

1 bow, quiver, and arrows.  Bow and quiver used by mountain tribes and captured from them, Dec 20, 1904 near Perud Cata.  The heads of the arrows are poisoned. 


1 of 19 poisoned arrows.  Long bamboo shaft with wooden point inserted into the hollow end.  The other end is closed by a natural growth ring/node.  The point narrows to the tip and is darkened, possibly burnt, and sections are coated in an unknown substance (poison?).  The joint is lashed with a spiral of reed.
Curatorial Notes:
all of the wooden points are loose and detach from the shaft easily.  Therefore, the pairings might not be accurate.  Some points were extremely loose..

The card indicates 19 arrows, 6 of which are metal tipped, but none of these were found.  All 19 found are poison tipped.

Complex spear (arrow?). Long bamboo shaft.  

The very distal end is wrapped with woven fiber. Fiber woven in such a ay to form bumps that stick out. This is then covered with an unknown substance.  

The next section of the shaft is wrapped around with a multi-strand section of braided fiber. It is wrapped tightly at first, but loosely later on. Near the end a small wooden dowel is attached with fiber cord. At the very end a metal point with a hollow tang and a barb is attached. One end of the dowel inserts into the hollow opening of the point. The other end of the dowel inserts into the distal end of the shaft, so that it forms a fore-shaft and then a point. 

Both ends of the dowel are tapered. The very end (proximal) has a carved groove forming a neck.
